descriptionChirho: To lay hands on someone with hostile intent, to arrest or seize by force; used of the arrest of Jesus (Matt 26:50; Mark 14:46; John 7:30, 44), the apostles (Acts 4:3; 5:18; 21:27), James by Herod (Acts 12:1), and the intent of Jewish leaders to seize Jesus (Luke 20:19; 21:12). Multilingual glosses consistently use forceful arrest vocabulary: arb: ألقوا (cast upon), deu: Hand anlegen (lay hand on), heb: שלח (send forth hand), kor: 놓다/내밀다 (lay/extend), spa: echar/poner (throw/put). This sense represents the violent or authoritative extension of physical force upon a person.

labelChirho: put upon, place on, throw on
descriptionChirho: To place, put, or throw something upon a surface or object; the physical action of laying one thing on another. Used of putting a patch on a garment (Matt 9:16; Luke 5:36), throwing garments on a colt (Mark 11:7), putting one's hand to the plow (Luke 9:62), and Paul not wishing to throw a restraint upon the Corinthians (1 Cor 7:35). Multilingual glosses center on placement: arb: يضع (place), eng: puts/throw on, heb: מניח/שם/השליך (set/place/throw), hin: लगाता/रखकर/डालूं (apply/place/throw), kor: 덮다/손을 댄 (cover/touch), spa: poner/echar (put/throw). Distinct from the seizure sense in lacking hostile intent — this is placement of objects, not arrest of persons.

Of natural forces (waves, storm) beating upon or breaking over something; used in Mark 4:37 where waves were breaking over the boat during the storm on the Sea of Galilee. Multilingual glosses reflect violent natural impact: arb: ارتفعت (rose up), eng: were throwing, heb: הכה (struck), hin: गिरती थीं (were falling), kor: 덮쳤다 (overwhelmed), spa: golpeaban (were striking). This is a figurative extension of the 'throw upon' meaning applied to impersonal natural forces rather than human agency.

To set one's mind upon something, to reflect deeply, or to break down emotionally; used in Mark 14:72 where Peter, after hearing the rooster crow and remembering Jesus' prediction of his denial, is described with this participle before weeping bitterly. This is a famous crux interpretum: glosses diverge significantly — arb: منهارا (collapsing), eng: breaking down, heb: פרץ (burst forth), hin: फूट पड़कर (bursting out), kor: 생각하며 (thinking/reflecting), spa: habiendo pensado en ello (having thought about it). Whether 'he broke down and wept' or 'reflecting on it he wept,' this intransitive middle-voice sense of turning thought or emotion inward is semantically distinct from all transitive physical meanings of the verb.

labelChirho: fall to one's share, belong to
descriptionChirho: Of property or inheritance falling to someone's portion; an impersonal intransitive use meaning 'what belongs to' or 'what is due to.' Used in the Parable of the Prodigal Son (Luke 15:12) where the younger son asks for the share of the estate 'falling to him.' Multilingual glosses confirm the inheritance/portion meaning: arb: اللائق (what is fitting/due), eng: falling (to one's share), heb: הנופל (the falling/accruing), hin: मिलने वाला (that which is to be received), kor: 돌아오는 (that which comes around to), spa: que me corresponde (that which corresponds to me). This impersonal intransitive usage is semantically distinct from all transitive uses of the verb.
